label: Claude Fable 5.2
output:
Peter, I'll answer Brenda's question through you, because we did almost exactly what you're recommending and reversed it seven months later.

For context, I'm HR manager at a logistics firm with about 340 staff across a Nairobi depot and a Mombasa one. They are mostly drivers, turn-boys, loaders and warehouse clerks, so the pay profile is similar to Brenda's line workers.

First, where I think you're right. Nine years of payroll shows in your post. The serial borrower who takes an advance every single month is real, and so is the leaver who goes owing. An informal scheme where people come to the HR office and explain themselves is a bad scheme. Ours was like that too, and Finance was right to object to it. Brenda's Finance Manager is right about hers as it stands.

But we closed ours in February 2025, after our Finance Manager made your argument almost word for word. We gave two months' notice and ran a financial literacy session with the SACCO. Here is what happened.

In the six months after closing, reception logged 61 calls from debt collectors and loan apps. Before that it was a handful. Some of the apps were calling supervisors, because staff had listed them as "referees". That is my main disagreement with you. You say the apps are the employee's own decision and own contract, and on paper they are. In practice the collection lands at the workplace, on people who never signed anything.

Unplanned absence on the two days after month-end went up. Our fleet manager tied at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers who were away "sorting out" loans.

One loader at the Mombasa depot had six apps running at once by the time he came to me, borrowing from one to pay another. It took us four months, working with payroll, to unwind it. That was far more of my time than approving advances ever was.

So people did adjust, as you say they always do. They adjusted by borrowing somewhere worse, and the cost came back to us through reception, fleet and supervisors.

On the SACCO, ours takes two to three weeks to process a loan and needs guarantors. That's fine for planned borrowing. It's useless when a child is sent home over school fees on a Tuesday. The literacy session was worth doing and I would do it again. But someone earning KES 28,000 a month can't budget their way to an emergency fund, however good the session is.

We reopened in September 2025, this time as a written policy:

- Maximum 40% of net pay.
- One advance per pay cycle.
- Repaid in full at the next payroll, so nothing rolls over.
- No fee, no interest.
- Requests go through the payroll portal, not my office.
- Before approval, payroll checks total deductions against the Employment Act limit of two-thirds of wages, so nobody ends up with nothing at month-end.

Since then we've had 55 to 70 requests a month, averaging around KES 9,000. That is roughly KES 500,000 to 630,000 out at any one time, all back at the next payroll. Recovery has been 100% except for two leavers, and the total written off for the year was about KES 14,000.

The 40% cap and full repayment speak to your "permanently one month behind" point. Someone can still take an advance every month, but they can't dig deeper, because the amount is capped and cleared each cycle. That is quite different from a loan app balance that grows.

Our Finance Manager, the one who pushed for closure, now defends the scheme himself. What changed his mind was that the exposure became a fixed ceiling he could put in the forecast in advance. His complaint had really been about the surprises.

Brenda, for the 18th, I'd take two things from this.

One is to concede the Finance Manager's point early. The informal scheme should go, and the question for the meeting is what replaces it. Propose something of the shape above: a cap, a frequency limit, full repayment at next payroll and an approval route that doesn't run through your office. Kiprono's point about the ceiling matches our experience exactly.

The other is to bring your own numbers. Pull the last 12 months from payroll:

- How many advances a month, and the average amount.
- How many people take one every month.
- How much has been written off when people left.

I suspect the write-off figure is small, and it's the one Finance fears most.

Then ask them to set that against what closure costs. Our problem was that the costs of advances sat on one line Finance could see. The costs of closing were spread across reception, fleet, supervisors and HR, so nobody added them up. Our missed runs alone cost more than a year of write-offs.

Peter, I don't expect to convert you, and I'd have agreed with you in January 2025. But we tried closing the window and it didn't go the way either of us would have predicted.

---

I wrote "a Nairobi depot and a Mombasa one" instead of Embakasi and Changamwe, since the two locations plus the headcount could identify the firm. The KES 500,000 to 630,000 figure is my own calculation from your request numbers. "Cost more than a year of write-offs" assumes each missed run cost well over KES 14,000, so check you're comfortable with both before posting.
